item.title: Market and competitor analysis with AI in one day instead of a month.
item.description:
```html

Good marketing analysis is the foundation of almost any new project. Until you understand who your audience is, who your competitors are, what their offers and prices are, there is simply nowhere to go. Previously, such analysis took two to three weeks, and sometimes a whole month of manual work. Now this process can be accelerated many times over thanks to neural networks. 

Hi! My name is Dmitry Satarov, I am the head of the agency "Hey, Startuper!" and a mentor for the course "Neural Networks for Marketing" at Yandex Practicum. When decent neural networks appeared in 2022–2023, I began to build a process that would allow marketing research to be performed much faster. I will share it in this article.

Read more ```

item.title: Pre-IPO of foreign IT and AI companies: explaining how the market works
item.description:
Early investors in Anthropic, SpaceX, or OpenAI made multiple returns, but not by buying shares on the IPO day. The main growth happened earlier, at the private funding stage, when these companies were not yet available to the broad market.

This stage is called Pre‑IPO — the last major round before going public. The article examines how the market for foreign Pre‑IPO IT and AI companies works, what its potential sources of returns are, and why the legal details of a deal are no less important than the well-known brands.

Learn more

item.title: Virtual employees instead of AI assistants: how agents learn to work inside the company
item.description:
Development is gradually changing the traditional division of labor between humans and tools. AI is taking on not just individual operations, but sequences of actions that previously required a specialist's involvement. However, as autonomy grows, the requirements for the system itself are also changing. An agent must understand the project context, know internal rules, and have access to the tools the team uses—not just search for information and write code. 

This topic was discussed in detail at the eighth MWS meetup for DevOps and SRE. Experts from MTC Web Services and Orion Soft showcased different aspects of the transition to agentic development and shared case studies on how AI is gradually turning into a virtual employee—an agent that operates without constant human supervision—and what needs to be changed in engineering processes to make this happen.

Read more

item.title: The end of fat margins for AI: all about pricing and cheap model costs.
item.description:
Recently, the AI sphere is not just declining, but is even entering an active stage of competition between several fronts — corporate AI (OpenAI and Anthropic, who are also competing with each other) versus open models (Qwen, GLM, DeepSeek).

Prices per token sometimes drop, and when they can't reduce the price, they create lightweight models with low cost. The reduction in inference cost has ceased to be merely a side effect of optimization and has become the main axis of competition. OpenAI's decision to lower prices on GPT 5.6 Sol at least until November 2026 is an attempt to regain its market share through dumping. Open models are no longer just catching up with closed ones in quality, but sometimes even surpass them in usage economics, making access to AI a utility service.

In this article, we will examine the impact of Qwen, GLM, and other open-source models, competition in the AI market, and finally figure out where the AI race has turned this time.

item.title: Ox Alpha (GLM-5.3-Flash). What was that?
item.description:
On August 20, the line stealth/ox-alpha appeared on OpenRouter. No model card, not even a hint of who released it. The provider was listed as "Anonymous." Price – zero. Context – a million. The platform warned: we are not the owner of this model, we just route requests.

Six days later, the anonymous had a name, tens of trillions of processed tokens, and half a million developers who had already poured working code into it. Spoiler that’s no longer a spoiler: it turned out to be GLM-5.3-Flash from China’s Z.ai.

But the journey from "something unknown" to "frontier model" was dramatic and deserves a breakdown. And since I personally stared at that thread for almost a week, refreshing the feed like a man possessed – I’ll tell you what happened there, in order.

Read more

item.title: From Copilot to AI Factory: Where AI Is Already Paying Off and What Should a Developer Focus On?
item.description:
Sometimes it happens that a company buys artificial intelligence before it has time to understand what it needs it for, and yes, it is a tribute to chaos and the fear of falling out of the race. The CEO has already heard at a forum that agents will replace half the office; the innovation director has already promised a pilot by the end of the quarter; HR has ordered a webinar on prompts for employees, because any technological change in Russia first and foremost requires a webinar; and the CFO sits in a meeting, flipping through a presentation, trying to find the slide where all this new digital life finally turns into money. Only that slide isn't there yet. But by lunchtime, the neural network has written a congratulation to the CEO, and by evening, an order has appeared to create a working group — the implementation, one might say, has been a success, everyone is happy.

I am deliberately exaggerating, but only slightly (I expressed myself very cautiously). Artificial intelligence is already bringing quite tangible benefits to business: it reduces the time for processing inquiries, brings newcomers up to the level of more experienced employees, manages inventory, detects defects, predicts breakdowns, and parses documents faster than people who, just yesterday, had to transfer data from one window to another while maintaining the expression of someone engaged in intellectual labor. However, money appears not where the model better simulates an interlocutor, but where it is embedded in a repetitive operation and is accountable to a metric that is not impressed by the quality of a demo or the number of parameters: time, cost, error, downtime, turnover, or profit.

Read more

item.title: Yet Another English — and yes, another site for learning English, well what can you do?
item.description:
Well, as you probably figured out, I named the service that way to immediately close the main objection (hehe). Yes, I know there are thousands of them — and I made another one, and I'll explain why later.

My English is mediocre, around B1 (but for a product manager position, you usually need a higher level, you know). I watch YouTube in English to improve it and constantly come across unfamiliar words. Writing them into a spreadsheet, loading them into Anki — I was too lazy. What I wanted was this: drop a link to a video — words at my level would automatically be pulled from the subtitles and get queued for repetition.

I work a lot, so in the evenings I usually have 1–2 hours. After a couple of months of such evenings (595 commits), a trainer came out: a PWA on React, data lives in IndexedDB on the user's side, plus a dictionary and various exercises.

From a “website of the AI era” you expect there to be a wrapper around a chatbot, RAG, and all that stuff, you get the idea. For me it turned out the opposite: the LLM here is a contractor for two narrow tasks, while the main work is done by frequency lists, an algorithm from the '90s, and Claude as a workhorse. That's actually what this article, or series of articles, will be about.

Read more

item.title: Blind search for new particles (and not only particles), part 2: pharmaceutical domain and what was found in it
item.description:
But what if the scientific hypothesis search system doesn’t find a new answer—but instead reveals that the question itself is posed in the wrong parameters? That keeps me up at night… And another thought sparks new ideas: what if everything is already known for known parameters (even though there are gaps in knowledge that also need to be filled)? That’s why I introduced unknown adaptive parameters, which can then be computed—and these are precisely what provide new directions, candidates, and theories, and an enormous multitude of them, more than the number of atoms in the universe! But the entire space, based on my observations, divides into regions, sectors, zones! In this article, we experimentally connected the pharmaceutical domain to our architecture and ran a blind search, obtaining millions of candidates (we’re not yet sure what to do with them). The result was interesting—incomprehensible to a non‑specialist, but I think it’s significant). The system: — independently rediscovered already known therapeutic directions—this served as a positive control; — found several hundred target × modality × disease combinations for which we did not detect exact prior art in targeted searches (it’s impossible to scan the entire space—it’s huge, like the Bitcoin range, only even larger); — on the conflicting P2X7/Parkinson data, our system refused to choose the “correct” publication and determined that the existing parameters are insufficient (debugging may be needed); — proposed an additional research‑local coordinate pathophysiologic_endotype, while preventing it from automatically entering the canonical registry; — and on the second conflict, TLR7/Alzheimer, something even more interesting happened: the new parameters looked very informative within the sample, but permutation/LOO‑check showed that the effect does not generalize. The hypothesis was halted.

So the chain is: REDISCOVERY → RESEARCH GAP → AXIS INCOMPLETE → SELF‑CORRECTION. The article contains all candidates, formulas, real numbers, a reproducible P2X7 case, the discovered defect in the causal‑readiness gate, and how we fixed it.

Read more

I explain how I connected Codex and Claude Code with a task tracker, why a simple retry after a timeout once created duplicates, and why a separate deterministic layer is needed between the LLM and API.

item.title: Where did AI come from and what does the word perceptron have to do with it
item.description:
The journey from the first attempt to model a neuron to the systems that today write code and carry on conversations took less than 70 years — and nearly collapsed halfway through. We explore how Rosenblatt's perceptron almost buried the idea of neural networks, what brought it back to life, and why transformers changed everything.

Read more

item.title: LLM confidently lies about your microcontroller
item.description:
I asked an AI to write firmware for a board with a small display. The code was perfect: compiled on the first try, flashed without errors. But on the screen – just color noise.

The problem isn't the code – the model simply doesn't know your board. Which pins are used for what, which clock configuration actually works, which HAL calls silently do nothing – all of this is scattered across a datasheet of a hundred pages, the manufacturer's wiki, and the evening of debugging you spent on it.

And how to solve this?

Read more
